canonicalExplanation.summary: An **iterator** marks a position in a container, like a smart pointer into it. Ranges are **half-open**: `[begin, end)`. `begin()` is the first element, and `end()` is **one past the last**, a boundary you compare against but **never dereference**. An empty range has `begin() == end()`, so loops run zero times. Iterators can be **invalidated** by operations that change the container: `push_back` that reallocates a vector invalidates **all** its iterators, and `erase` invalidates iterators **at and after** the erased position. So `erase` returns the **next valid iterator**: use it. For map, erasing one element only invalidates iterators to that element.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner removes odd numbers with `for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) if (*it % 2) v.erase(it);`. It crashes or skips elements, because `it` is invalid right after erase. An algorithm processes every vector element from begin up to but not including end and performs zero steps when begin equals end. In this lesson you'll repair an invalidated-iterator defect and document the governing container operation.


examples.title: From begin up to, not including, end
examples.situation: An algorithm processes every vector element from begin up to but not including end and performs zero steps when begin equals end.
walkthrough: **Processes every vector element from begin:** sum starts at v.begin() and will add each element.
**Up to but not including end:** the loop condition it != v.end() stops before dereferencing end.
**Performs zero steps when begin equals end:** sum of an empty vector will return 0 with no special case.
examples.result: The loop visits each element once and handles empty input naturally.

examples.title: The skipping erase
examples.situation: remove_odds on {1, 3, 4} leaves {3, 4} in a version that always does ++it.
walkthrough: After erasing 1, erase returned an iterator to 3.
Advance only when nothing was erased (or use std::erase_if).
examples.result: All odd numbers are removed, including adjacent ones.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The end iterator refers to the last element and can be dereferenced before a loop stops.
misconceptions.correction: end() is one past the last element. It marks where the range stops and must never be dereferenced.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what does *v.end() give?

analogy.example: An iterator range is like **reading a book from page 1 up to the back cover**: you read every page, but the back cover (end) isn't a page. Tearing out a page (erase) renumbers everything after it, so ask the book "what's the next page now?" (erase's return value).
usefulFor: remembering the back cover isn't a page
ask for the next page after tearing
limitations: Books don't move to new shelves; growing vectors do.
An empty book: front cover = back cover.

steps.explanation: Processing starts at begin and will stop at end.
erase returns the next valid iterator instead of invalidating the loop.
Every element up to but not including end was processed.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a safe erase loop. Step 1, Start: v is {1, 3, 4}; it is -> 1. Processing starts at begin and will stop at end. Step 2, Erase: v is {3, 4}; it is -> 3 (returned). erase returns the next valid iterator instead of invalidating the loop. Step 3, Finish: v is {4}; it is end. Every element up to but not including end was processed.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write a loop that removes all empty strings from a std::vector<std::string> using erase's return value, then rewrite it with std::erase_if. Test {"", "", "a", "", "b"} and an empty vector.
scaffold: Adjacent empties are the tricky case.

farTransfer.prompt: Remove entries with value 0 from a std::map<std::string, int> during iteration, using the iterator returned by erase. Document which iterators map::erase invalidates and contrast with vector.
scaffold: it = m.erase(it) works for map too.
Only the erased element's iterators are invalidated.

remediation.explanation: For every loop that changes its container ask: **which operation invalidates which iterators, and where does my loop get its next valid iterator?**

recap.summary: To work with iterators safely, treat ranges as half-open [begin, end) and never dereference end, rely on begin == end meaning empty, know that vector reallocation invalidates all iterators and erase invalidates the erased position onward, and continue loops from the iterator erase returns (or use std::erase_if).
